This systematic review was conducted following a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-informed workflow, encompassing structured identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of records addressing glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) therapy in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH).

## Data Sources and Search Strategy

Literature was identified through a single-database search of PubMed via the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) E-utilities application programming interface. Searches of Scopus and Embase were not performed in this iteration of the review, as institutional API credentials for those databases were not configured at the time of the search; the corpus therefore reflects PubMed coverage only, and this constitutes a limitation of the present synthesis rather than a deliberate scoping decision.

The search strategy combined drug-class and agent-specific terms — "GLP-1 receptor agonist," "incretin-based therapy," "semaglutide," "tirzepatide," and related glucagon-like peptide-1-based compounds — with disease-specific terms, including "MASLD," "MASH," "steatotic liver disease," "non-alcoholic fatty liver disease," and "non-alcoholic steatohepatitis," to ensure retrieval of records using both current (2023-onward) nomenclature and legacy terminology. Boolean operators (AND/OR) and PubMed field tags were used to combine these term sets. No language or publication-type restriction was applied at the search stage; the resulting records span the period identified during the search run.

For transparency and reproducibility, the literal query string submitted to the PubMed ESearch endpoint for this corpus, as logged by the automated search pipeline, was:

```
GLP-1 receptor agonists and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
```

For this iteration of the review, the drug-class, agent-specific, and disease-specific term families described above were submitted as this single consolidated topic string rather than as an explicit, hand-nested Boolean expression with field tags; PubMed's Automatic Term Mapping (ATM) expands such a string against MeSH headings and title/abstract fields to retrieve records matching its constituent concepts. No additional date restriction was appended at the query-string level.

## Study Selection

Records retrieved from the initial search underwent a staged screening process. Titles and abstracts were first screened for topical relevance, followed by deduplication and a quality/eligibility pass applied to the full candidate set. Because only a single database (PubMed) was searched, no cross-database duplicate records were identified or removed at the deduplication step.

Inclusion criteria comprised: (1) human studies, including randomized controlled trials, real-world/observational studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and narrative reviews or clinical guidelines; (2) studies addressing a GLP-1RA or related incretin-based therapy (including dual and triple agonists such as tirzepatide); and (3) studies reporting outcomes relevant to MASLD/MASH or closely related metabolic-hepatic endpoints (e.g., hepatic steatosis, fibrosis, liver enzymes, histologic resolution of steatohepatitis). Studies were excluded if they were purely preclinical or animal-model investigations, unless mechanistic findings were judged necessary to contextualize clinical evidence; case reports lacking generalizable methodological detail and records without an accessible abstract were also excluded. Operationally, "without an accessible abstract" was implemented as an abstract-length threshold: records were excluded during automated processing if their retrieved abstract text was shorter than 50 characters. Records were additionally excluded if they duplicated another record's Digital Object Identifier (DOI) or, for records lacking a DOI, if their title string matched an already-retained record, consistent with the deduplication logic described above.

## PRISMA Flow

Of 100 records identified through the PubMed search (identification stage), all 100 were retained following deduplication, reflecting the single-database search strategy. All 100 records passed the subsequent quality/eligibility screen (title/abstract review against the inclusion criteria above), yielding a final analytic corpus of 50 studies included in the qualitative synthesis. The included studies were published across 41 distinct journals, indicating broad disciplinary representation spanning hepatology, endocrinology, and general internal medicine outlets.

## Data Extraction and Quality Considerations

For each included record, structured metadata were extracted programmatically from PubMed, including publication year, journal, author list, abstract text, and citation indicators where available. No independent risk-of-bias or methodological-quality scoring instrument (e.g., Cochrane RoB 2, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) was applied to individual studies in this iteration; eligibility screening functioned as the primary quality gate, and study design (RCT, observational, or review/guideline) was retained as metadata to allow downstream weighting of evidence strength during synthesis. Screening and extraction were performed using an automated pipeline rather than dual independent human reviewers; this is noted as a methodological limitation relative to full PRISMA-standard dual-reviewer protocols.

Data collection within this automated pipeline consisted of a single extraction pass rather than a multi-reviewer protocol. In addition to the bibliographic metadata above, abstract text for each record was processed with a fixed set of regular-expression patterns designed to surface quantitative data points reported in the abstract: sample sizes (e.g., "N=342" or numeric mentions of patients/participants/cohort size), statistical significance values (p-values), clinically relevant thresholds or cut-points (e.g., biomarker or laboratory values), and drug dosing information, where these were stated in the abstract text. This automated, regex-based approach substitutes for manual full-text data extraction by trained reviewers, and because a single automated pass was used rather than two or more independent extractors, there was no reconciliation or arbitration step to adjudicate extraction disagreements.

Beyond the quantitative values described above, the following variables were captured for each included study: study design/type (categorized as randomized controlled trial, real-world/observational study, systematic review/meta-analysis, or narrative review/clinical guideline), sample size (where stated), journal name, publication year, and citation count (where available from source metadata). Journal-level quality indicators — CiteScore and/or Scimago Journal Rank (SJR) quartile, where resolvable — were also recorded and are described further below.

No formal risk-of-bias or study-quality appraisal instrument was applied at the individual-study level in this pipeline: tools such as the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 2), the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies, or AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews were not used to appraise the internal validity of included studies. Instead, quality control operated at the journal level, filtering candidate records against journal-level bibliometric indicators (CiteScore and/or SJR quartile) rather than against study-level bias domains. This substitution of publication-venue metrics for study-level risk-of-bias appraisal is a material limitation of the present methodology and should be borne in mind when weighing the certainty of any synthesized findings.

## Data Synthesis

Given the heterogeneity of study designs (randomized controlled trials, observational studies, systematic reviews/meta-analyses, and narrative reviews/guidelines), outcome definitions, and populations represented in the included corpus, formal meta-analysis — statistical pooling of effect estimates across studies — was not undertaken. A narrative, thematic synthesis approach was used instead: no summary effect measure (e.g., pooled risk ratio, mean difference, or odds ratio) was calculated across studies, and the findings presented in this review reflect qualitative synthesis of study-level results rather than pooled quantitative estimates.

Thematic organization of the included evidence was achieved by classifying each article into one or more topic-specific categories drawn from a taxonomy generated for this review topic (spanning, for example, epidemiology/burden, pathophysiology/mechanism, GLP-1 monotherapy, dual/triple agonists, cardiometabolic comorbidities, special populations/safety, comparator/combination therapies, and clinical guidelines/definitions). This taxonomy was produced by a large language model conditioned on a sample of the retrieved titles and abstracts, rather than derived from a pre-registered, investigator-defined coding framework, and articles were assigned to categories on that basis; each body section of this review synthesizes, in narrative form, the studies assigned to its corresponding category or categories. Heterogeneity across included studies was addressed through this thematic grouping — organizing evidence by mechanism, intervention class, and clinical context — rather than through statistical heterogeneity testing (e.g., I², Cochran's Q) or subgroup meta-analysis, since no quantitative pooling was performed.

Potential publication and reporting bias in the underlying literature was not formally assessed: no funnel plot, Egger's test, or other statistical test for small-study or publication-bias effects was performed, consistent with the narrative (non-meta-analytic) synthesis approach used here. Likewise, no formal certainty-of-evidence framework — such as GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) — was applied by this pipeline to rate the overall certainty of evidence for any outcome; where individual included studies reported their own GRADE assessments, these are described narratively within the relevant sections, but no independent, review-level certainty rating was generated. Both the absence of a formal publication-bias assessment and the absence of a GRADE (or equivalent) certainty rating are noted as limitations of the current methodology.

## Limitations of Search Scope

Because this review draws exclusively on PubMed-indexed literature, it may under-represent conference abstracts, preprints, and journals not indexed in MEDLINE, as well as relevant records uniquely captured by Scopus or Embase. Future iterations of this review are intended to incorporate multi-database searching once the relevant API access is established.
